summary: Puerto Rico's northeast-tip faro, built by Spain around 1880 and lit in 1882; its lantern was damaged in the 1932 hurricane, and it now lies in a nature reserve.

lens.note: Westinghouse four-way revolving beacon installed after the 1932 hurricane (nomination); USLHS lists the current optic as DCB-24.

structures.note: Cylindrical tower with a brick and stone lantern, 13.35 m to the top of the lantern (nomination). USLHS gives 39 feet from base to lantern centre; the 1901 Board gives the light 260 feet above sea level.
One-story keepers' dwelling built for one first- and third-class keeper; '1880' inscribed over the doorway.

access.note: Visits by reservation on a tour of Las Cabezas de San Juan Nature Reserve (LighthouseFriends); the nomination classes the light as occupied, restricted access.

visit.note: Grounds, dwelling and tower open during reserve tours; reservations through the Conservation Trust of Puerto Rico.

facts.agency: Conservation Trust of Puerto Rico (owner, per LighthouseFriends)

events.note: First plans commissioned; construction begins early 1877 but the first project is later dropped.
Begun, per the Light-House Board's 1901 report (finished 1880).
Finished, per the 1901 Board report; '1880' inscription over the doorway.
Light officially lit 2 May 1882 (nomination). The station record gives 1882; USLHS gives 1885.
Third-order Fresnel lens installed, per USLHS (conflicts with the nomination's 1881 Sautter lens).
Party from USS Amphitrite takes the light on 6 August during the Spanish-American War; a naval cadet dies of an accidental wound; skirmish on 8 August (LighthouseFriends only).
Keeper Manuel del Olmo and assistant Augustin S. Cruz rescue a man from an overturned fishing boat on 12 September.
Oil changed to incandescent oil vapour.
Original lens removed, per the nomination's evidence; replaced by a fourth-order Barbier & Bernard lens (50 cm).
Characteristic changed from fixed white with alternating flashes to group-flashing white.
Minor cracks reported at Cape San Juan in the Bulletin's account of autumn 1918 earthquakes.
Hurricane (night of 26-27 September per LighthouseFriends) severely damages the lantern and lens; a Westinghouse four-way revolving beacon replaces the optic.
Conservation Trust of Puerto Rico acquires 321 acres on the San Juan headlands; the lighthouse lies within the reserve.
Listed on the National Register of Historic Places, 22 October 1981.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The nomination says the light was officially lit on 2 May 1882. The Light-House Board's 1901 report says it was begun in 1878 and finished in 1880. The USLHS record gives 1885 for the station and the lens. The record's 1882 matches the nomination's lighting date; the USLHS 1885 date may be the date of the station's establishment on the register. Not resolved.

LighthouseFriends says construction began only in 1881 (against the nomination's early-1877 start and the 1901 Board's 1878 start), and gives 2 May 1882 for the lighting, which matches the nomination. The story gives the Board's, the nomination's and LighthouseFriends' dates and does not choose between them.

notes_for_editor: (1) Dates disagree: nomination lit 2 May 1882 after a March 1882 delivery; Board 1901 'begun 1878, finished 1880' at 16,300 pesos; LighthouseFriends says construction began in 1881 and the light was lit 2 May 1882; USLHS 'Year Established 1885' with a third-order Fresnel lens 'installed 1885'; station record first_lit 1882. The story gives the nomination's date and the Board's, and does not choose. (2) Lens: nomination says a 1881 Sautter, Lemonnier third-order lens was removed in 1916 and replaced by a fourth-order Barbier & Bernard; LighthouseFriends says a fourth-order Fresnel replaced it in 1916; USLHS says third-order Fresnel 1885 and current DCB-24. The station record's lens is null. (3) The 1898 Atwater episode rests on LighthouseFriends alone. A Chronicling America check was attempted on 2026-10-22 and returned HTTP 520 from loc.gov; no newspaper or Navy report was confirmed. Treat as unverified until checked. (4) Automation: the record says automated in 1975 (Wikidata); no readable source gives that date, so the story does not state it. A Bulletin 1938 passage about one keeper is garbled in the OCR and was not quoted. (5) Record 'ownership unknown' vs LighthouseFriends: Conservation Trust of Puerto Rico. The Trust's 1975 purchase of 321 acres is from LighthouseFriends. (6) The NRHP cached copy has only continuation sheets 43-47; sheets 1-42 (description summary and earlier pages) were not in the cache. (7) HAER PR-40 is at loc.gov, which returned 403 on fetch and is not used. (8) The 1901 Board volume is cited by scan page (printed page not confirmed). (9) Roster: USLHS lines copied as printed; LighthouseFriends adds Jose Perez Castillo (1935 to at least 1941). Spanish-era keepers before 1901 are not named in any source read. The living-people rule applies to Angel Rodriguez and Robert Konitz (USLHS roster lines only, no personal details). (10) Units: the 1901 Board gives the light's height as 260 feet above sea level and visibility as 18 miles (unspecified nautical or statute); the record gives 11 nautical miles range (ENC); not reconciled. (11) Record access 'public' vs LighthouseFriends: reservation required for reserve tours. (12) Fact-check pass 2026-10-22: the 1782 Abbad peaks are printed in the nomination as Loquillo and Laivonito, so the story uses that spelling; the Bulletin 1913 spells the assistant Augustin, the USLHS roster Agustin; the story uses both with a note. The 1901 Board's 'near the town of Fajardo' is in the OCR as 'near the tmim of Fajardo' and was not quoted; the story says 'near Fajardo' and cites USLHS for the town. The 'Konitz' and 'Rodriguez' roster lines are USLHS-only and carry no personal detail.
